title: AI services: Deployment gaps create consulting opportunity
desc: Treats enterprise implementation as a partner-led services market, with developer and private-equity alliances creating both cooperation and competition.

kps.k: The cluster frames enterprise AI deployment—not model access alone—as a professional-services opportunity.
kps.d: OpenAI, Anthropic and their partners argue that businesses need implementation expertise to turn capable models into operational value. Their proposed response combines embedded engineers, workflow redesign, systems integration and organisational change. This shifts the debate from what AI can produce to whether institutions can incorporate it into daily work; it does not establish that model capability has ceased to constrain adoption.

qs.q: Across those deployments, one pattern has become increasingly clear: the next stage of enterprise AI will be defined by how effectively businesses can deploy this technology into real-world use cases, and how well we and our Alliance partner ecosystem can help them.
qs.a: OpenAI launches the OpenAI Deployment Company to help businesses build around intelligence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: According to the partners, the effort is designed to address a growing bottleneck in the AI industry, which is the lack of professional experts who have the skills to integrate the technology within real-world business operations.
qs.a: OpenAI's $10bn 'Deployment Company' joint venture with TPG, Brookfield, Advent and Bain Capital · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Reported adoption and return gaps motivate the services strategy, but do not demonstrate its effectiveness.
kps.d: Techloy reports that about two-thirds of nearly 2,000 employees surveyed by McKinsey the previous summer said their organisations had not begun enterprise-wide AI scaling; more than half of nearly 4,500 CEOs surveyed by PwC reported little or no financial benefit. Separately, Shapiro cites a reported 2025 MIT finding that 95% of organisations saw no measurable generative-AI return. These accounts measure different things and cannot be pooled. They support concern about adoption and returns, not a causal finding that consulting resolves either problem. The European-bank example describes exploration of potential applications, not measured deployment gains.

qs.q: A McKinsey survey of nearly 2,000 employees last summer found that about two-thirds said their organisations had not yet begun scaling AI across the enterprise.
qs.a: OpenAI and Anthropic Turn to Consulting Firms to Help Businesses Adopt AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: The scramble follows a year of evidence that capability alone was not converting; MIT researchers reported in 2025 that, despite tens of billions of dollars in enterprise spending, 95 percent of organizations were seeing no measurable return on generative AI.
qs.a: Zack Shapiro on X: 'The Two Clocks' — the bottleneck has moved from AI capability to institutional absorption, and absorption is the professional-services opportunity · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The operating model combines partner-led consulting with deployment capacity controlled by AI developers.
kps.d: OpenAI’s Frontier Alliances assign BCG and McKinsey primarily strategic and operating-model roles, while Accenture and Capgemini handle broader technical integration. OpenAI also announced a majority-controlled Deployment Company with more than $4 billion in initial investment and an agreement to acquire Tomoro, expected to add approximately 150 specialists. Anthropic’s separate venture reportedly has approximately $1.5 billion in committed capital. These announcements establish investment and delivery plans, not successful outcomes. Tomoro’s agreement remained subject to closing conditions. Earlier reporting also distinguished—or inconsistently described—OpenAI’s $10 billion valuation and planned capital injection; neither figure establishes Tomoro’s purchase price.

qs.q: BCG and McKinsey are positioned primarily as strategy and operating model partners, helping leadership teams figure out where and how to deploy agents at scale.
qs.a: OpenAI partners with McKinsey, BCG, Accenture, and Capgemini to push its Frontier AI agent platform · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: The OpenAI Deployment Company is majority-owned and controlled by OpenAI, giving customers a unified experience whether they work with OpenAI, the OpenAI Deployment Company, or both.
qs.a: OpenAI launches the OpenAI Deployment Company to help businesses build around intelligence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Private-equity partnerships supply distribution and transformation incentives as well as capital.
kps.d: OpenAI says its investment and consulting partners sponsor more than 2,000 businesses, while Bain promises its PE clients priority access to joint deployment work. Reporting describes investor portfolios as initial customers before expansion into the wider mid-market. Sponsors and consultants expect gains through automation, growth and operational redesign; the portfolio reach is a prospective sales channel, not evidence of adoption or returns. The ventures also serve the labs’ enterprise-revenue ambitions amid competition from Anthropic, OpenAI and cloud incumbents.

qs.q: The OpenAI Deployment Company's investment and consulting partners sponsor more than 2,000 businesses around the world, and its consulting and integrator partners work with many thousands more.
qs.a: OpenAI launches the OpenAI Deployment Company to help businesses build around intelligence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: They’ll initially target their own portfolio companies, before trying to expand and target other midsized enterprises in areas such as healthcare, financial services, manufacturing and retail.
qs.a: OpenAI's $10bn 'Deployment Company' joint venture with TPG, Brookfield, Advent and Bain Capital · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The services turn makes consultants both partners and potential competitors, with disagreement over how novel the model is.
kps.d: Goldman Sachs’ Marc Nachmann distinguishes Anthropic’s embedded engineering from traditional consulting; analyst Holger Mueller argues that both ventures nevertheless resemble consultancies. Fortune’s Nick Lichtenberg predicts that model ownership and implementation capacity could undercut conventional consulting fees, but supplies no demonstrated price comparison. Mitch Ashley warns that OpenAI’s internal services capacity competes with the systems-integrator channel it needs. Jeremy Kahn similarly identifies a prospective threat to SaaS incumbents that depend on those same implementation partners; investor concerns do not establish widespread software replacement.

qs.q: Nachmann told CNBC the new entity won’t act like a traditional consulting firm, but instead embed Anthropic’s engineers within its customer’s teams, so they can help them to redesign their workflows and integrate AI agents into core business processes.
qs.a: OpenAI's $10bn 'Deployment Company' joint venture with TPG, Brookfield, Advent and Bain Capital · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: The Anthropic venture offers PE sponsors a turnkey alternative to hiring Big Three consultants at what is likely to be a fraction of the cost.
qs.a: Anthropic takes shot at consulting industry in joint venture with Wall Street giants · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Vendor-led deployment raises a trade-off between close technical support and customer control.
kps.d: OpenAI predicts that proximity to its research and product teams will produce systems that improve as models evolve. Tobias Mann instead interprets deployment services as protecting demand for OpenAI’s models and warns about price exposure; his reported doubling of GPT-5.5 token prices does not establish doubled workload costs, given OpenAI’s claim of possible token savings. Shapiro separately reports Alex Karp’s argument that customers should control their compute, models and data rather than transfer competitive advantage to deployment vendors. Practically, these positions make integration benefits, ongoing costs and control over AI infrastructure distinct procurement questions.

qs.q: The OpenAI Deployment Company FDEs will be able to build for where OpenAI's frontier capabilities are headed, giving customers systems designed to improve as new models, tools, and deployment patterns come online.
qs.a: OpenAI launches the OpenAI Deployment Company to help businesses build around intelligence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Karp said enterprise customers want to own the means of production behind their AI, their compute, models, data, and competitive edge, and dismissed vendor deployment ventures as arrangements that transfer that edge to a third party.
qs.a: Zack Shapiro on X: 'The Two Clocks' — the bottleneck has moved from AI capability to institutional absorption, and absorption is the professional-services opportunity · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The broader professional-services implication is a possible shift toward delivered outcomes and accountable judgment.
kps.d: Lichtenberg links the ventures to Julien Bek’s prediction that AI businesses will sell outcomes such as legal services, financial analysis and insurance processing rather than software licences. Shapiro argues that briefing quality constrains output and predicts that professional value will migrate from skilled production toward judgment under uncertainty. Tomoro likewise presents deployment as AI embedded alongside human judgment. These are business-model and professional-value propositions, not demonstrated earnings trends or evidence that the ventures already deliver legal work as ALSPs.

qs.q: Sequoia partner Julien Bek argued in April that the world’s next great company won’t sell software at all, but outcomes: legal services, financial analysis, insurance processing delivered by AI while billed like consulting.
qs.a: Anthropic takes shot at consulting industry in joint venture with Wall Street giants · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Zack Shapiro, “The Input Layer,” published on X, March 25, 2026, on why the model’s output is only as good as the briefing it receives.
qs.a: Zack Shapiro on X: 'The Two Clocks' — the bottleneck has moved from AI capability to institutional absorption, and absorption is the professional-services opportunity · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that enterprise AI’s immediate commercial opportunity lies in deployment services rather than model access alone, and materially develops it by identifying concrete delivery and distribution models. Across the sources, the recurring rationale is that enterprises need workflow redesign, systems integration, embedded engineering, change management, effective briefing and accountable professional judgment to convert technical capability into operational value. The sources further show how AI developers are assembling that capacity through consulting alliances and private-equity-backed ventures, with investor portfolios providing prospective customer channels. Material variation concerns who should control delivery and how disruptive the model will be: some reporting presents established consultants as essential partners; other analysis predicts AI-native, model-owning services firms could compete with or undercut traditional consultancies and SaaS vendors; and Shapiro reports a countervailing concern that vendor-led deployment may transfer control over compute, models, data and competitive advantage away from customers. The evidence establishes investment, partnerships and strategic intent, but reported cost advantages, returns, displacement and a shift from software licences to delivered outcomes remain forecasts rather than demonstrated results. Because these are curated sources, this alignment should not be treated as representative of market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: Today the AI company announced partnerships with Boston Consulting Group, McKinsey & Co., Accenture, and Capgemini that will see the consulting firms helping sell and implement OpenAI’s new Frontier AI agent platform.
qs.a: OpenAI partners with McKinsey, BCG, Accenture, and Capgemini to push its Frontier AI agent platform · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: The venture, backed by approximately $1.5 billion in committed capital, is designed to embed Anthropic’s engineers and models directly into the core operations of mid-size businesses, according to the _Wall Street Journal_ citing people familiar with the matter.
qs.a: Anthropic takes shot at consulting industry in joint venture with Wall Street giants · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources support the proposition that the principal enterprise-AI opportunity lies in implementation services rather than model access alone. Across the records, the common rationale is that enterprises need embedded engineering, use-case selection, workflow redesign, systems integration and change management to move from pilots to production. The announced partnerships, deployment company and Tomoro acquisition give this thesis a concrete operating model involving AI-developer control, consulting partners and private-equity-backed distribution. Material variation concerns the model’s risks and evidentiary status, not its basic direction: reported adoption and return gaps motivate the strategy but do not show that consulting has solved them; some commentary also warns that developer-owned delivery teams may compete with systems integrators and increase customer dependence or cost exposure. These selected sources therefore support the proposition while treating many claimed benefits as prospective rather than demonstrated; they should not be read as representing all legal-tech vendors.

qs.q: “Microsoft, Google, and AWS already reach those buyers through systems integrator relationships and partner-led implementation OpenAI hasn’t built.”  “Building that bench in-house puts OpenAI in direct competition with the SI channel it would otherwise need,” Ashley said.
qs.a: Tomoro Acquired by the OpenAI Deployment Company — ~150 Forward Deployed Engineers Transfer · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources support the proposition that the principal enterprise-AI bottleneck has shifted toward deployment and institutional integration, creating a professional-services market around embedded engineering, workflow redesign, systems integration and change management. They describe concrete partner-led structures—including consulting alliances, developer-controlled deployment companies, acquisitions and private-equity distribution channels—and cite reported scaling and return gaps as the motivation. Material internal variation concerns who should control delivery and capture value: some sources frame AI developers and consultants as complementary, while others anticipate competition with traditional consultancies, systems integrators and SaaS vendors. Karp’s reported preference for customer-controlled infrastructure and warnings about vendor dependence, pricing and channel conflict qualify rather than reject the services proposition. The evidence is strongest for investment, organisational design and intended delivery models; claims that these ventures will improve returns, lower costs, displace incumbents or shift revenue from licences to delivered outcomes remain predictions rather than demonstrated results.
